title: Three clients in Serbia and one in Bosnia asked us to provide a risk quantification report in euros — how much financial loss a specific vulnerability exposes them to — and we have no methodology for that; it's becoming a dealbreaker in contract negotiations.

record.text: Three clients in Serbia and one in Bosnia asked us to provide a risk quantification report in euros — how much financial loss a specific vulnerability exposes them to — and we have no methodology for that; it's becoming a dealbreaker in contract negotiations.
record.detail: Four clients — three in Serbia and one in Bosnia — have asked us to attach a euro figure to each finding in our SecAudit reports. They want to be able to tell their board: this vulnerability could cost us this much. We understand why they ask. They need to justify remediation budgets. The problem is we have never done this and we are not sure our current data supports it. We have records of what the vulnerabilities were, we know roughly what downtime costs for a water utility or an electricity distributor, and we can find published incident cost studies from Western Europe. What we do not have is a repeatable calculation method that holds up when a procurement officer asks how we arrived at the number. We have looked at two published frameworks and found them either too abstract or built for IT environments where data breach costs dominate. Our clients care about production downtime, regulatory fines under Serbian energy law, and emergency response costs. We need a methodology we can apply consistently across different client types, document in a way that survives scrutiny, and run with our existing audit team without hiring a financial analyst.
